implementation_notes: The standard library canonicalizes comparable values for you: unique.Make returns a Handle[T] that is equal exactly when the values were equal, so comparison is a pointer comparison and the canonical copy is retained only while some handle refers to it. The handle is the flyweight, the canonical value is its intrinsic state, and extrinsic state goes into the struct that holds the handle. Prefer this over a hand-rolled map on Go 1.23 and later; keep a handle alive wherever you want the entry to survive, since Value() returns a copy rather than pinning the pool entry.
code_sketch:
type Glyph struct{ Name string; W, H int }        // intrinsic state, immutable

var a = unique.Make(Glyph{"A", 8, 12})            // canonical copy + handle
var b = unique.Make(Glyph{"A", 8, 12})
fmt.Println(a == b)                               // true: one shared value

type Cell struct{ G unique.Handle[Glyph]; X, Y int }  // extrinsic per cell
pitfalls: The handle owns the entry: calling Value() and dropping the handle lets the canonical copy be collected, after which the next Make clones again and deduplication silently stops.
Make hashes and copies the value, so interning high-cardinality or per-request data moves the memory into the pool instead of saving it.
Values held by a handle are shared: never mutate through Value()'s result, and remember a handle for a struct with a pointer field keeps everything it points to alive.

variants.name: Hand-rolled interning table (sync.Map or mutex-guarded map)
variants.implementation_notes: Before Go 1.23 - or whenever the pool must be keyed by an intrinsic key rather than canonicalized by value equality - the factory is a package-level sync.Map: LoadOrStore returns the instance that won the race, so concurrent callers agree on one canonical pointer; a plain map plus a mutex is faster for write-once, read-many pools because sync.Map's read path degrades under churn, and go4.org/intern is the community package that adds weak references and finalizers so unused entries can be collected. Keys must be comparable, and the pool retains every entry for the lifetime of the process unless it is bounded by hand.
pitfalls: A plain map is not safe for concurrent writes: two goroutines interning the same key without synchronization create two instances and break the identity invariant.
sync.Map is optimized for stable key sets read many times; for frequent inserts of new keys a mutex-guarded map (or sharded maps) is usually faster.
The pool is global state retained forever: with unbounded keys it is a leak. Bound it, shard by key space, or use go4.org/intern's weak-reference interning.
